ideas.title: Anthropic's Near-Trillion Valuation Is a Verdict on B2B Architecture
ideas.trend: Anthropic in talks this week to raise $30B at ~$950B valuation per Bloomberg May 12, surpassing OpenAI's $852B record; one year ago Anthropic was worth $61.5B
ideas.consensus: Anthropic is winning the AI race against OpenAI; the funding round reflects competitive parity
ideas.angle: The valuation premium over revenues isn't about the capability race. Anthropic's 100% B2B model creates enterprise switching costs that consumer distribution can't match. The market is pricing in stickiness, not features.

content_pack.x_longform:
Anthropic just became the most valuable AI company in the world without building a single consumer product.

Bloomberg reported this week that Anthropic is in talks to raise $30 billion at a valuation near $950 billion, clearing OpenAI's $852 billion record set in March. One year ago Anthropic was worth $61.5 billion. The valuation compounded 15x in twelve months.

The revenue story explains part of it. Annualized revenue hit $30 billion by April, up from roughly $3 billion at the end of 2025. Claude Code drove a significant share of the acceleration, with enterprise customers building AI-native development workflows locked to Claude's API behavior. Projections have moved toward $45 billion in ARR before the round closes.

A 10x revenue increase justifies a 10x valuation increase. It does not justify 15x.

The premium comes from the architecture.

Anthropic generates its entire revenue from B2B contracts, primarily API deals and multi-year enterprise agreements where the buyer is making a consequential technical decision. Google committed up to $40 billion. Amazon up to $25 billion. SpaceX opened Colossus 1 in Memphis. Anthropic now has access to 300 megawatts and over 220,000 NVIDIA GPUs. These are not portfolio bets on a promising startup. These are load-bearing dependencies.

Traditional software investors value B2B revenue at a higher multiple than consumer revenue for one reason: stickiness. Enterprise contracts do not churn on a Tuesday because a competitor released a better model. Enterprise buyers run 18-month security reviews. Data teams tune evals against specific model behavior. Engineering teams build pipelines that assume specific API response formats. Legal teams approve indemnification terms that reference specific model versions. Switching requires rebuilding all of it.

Consumer apps run in reverse. ChatGPT's user base is enormous. It is also voluntary. The default Gemini widget shipping on every new Android phone is one less reason to open ChatGPT. Consumer distribution erodes at the infrastructure layer.

OpenAI bet that consumer distribution is the most durable moat in AI. Anthropic refused to participate in that bet and built switching costs instead.

The market is now pricing the two strategies. OpenAI at $852 billion. Anthropic at $950 billion. B2B switching costs just cleared consumer brand for the first time in this cycle.

Oracle made the same bet in the early 1990s. No consumer product. No brand recognition outside enterprise IT. A customer base locked into database contracts they could not exit without rewriting their data layer from scratch. Oracle was not the best database. It was the one that became infrastructure. The moat was not the technology. It was that displacing Oracle meant rebuilding a company's core systems entirely. Most enterprises never tried.

By the time MySQL and PostgreSQL offered technically superior alternatives, Oracle had already compounded its relationships into dependencies that no superior product could dislodge at scale.

Anthropic is building the same position in the AI layer. Enterprise teams do not run Claude because it tops every benchmark. They run Claude because their systems are built around Claude, and replacing it means rebuilding the AI backbone of their product.

OpenAI built the consumer brand. Anthropic built the switching cost.

The switching cost compounds.

content_pack.substack_draft:
$950 billion at zero consumer accounts. That number is doing all the work in this story.

Bloomberg reported this week that Anthropic is in talks to raise at a valuation near $950 billion, which would make it more valuable than OpenAI. Anthropic has no consumer product. Its entire revenue, now at $30 billion annualized, comes from enterprise API contracts and multi-year agreements where the buyer is making a multi-year architecture decision.

Most people are framing this as a competitive horse race: Anthropic beating OpenAI in the funding round, the safety-first lab winning the money. I am not sure that is the right frame. What the $950B actually tells you is that the market has decided enterprise AI infrastructure is worth a higher multiple than consumer AI distribution. That is a significant verdict on the question everyone in AI has been arguing about for two years.

The interesting question is whether it holds. Consumer distribution in software has historically been winner-take-most, and OpenAI has a head start in the consumer layer that is hard to replicate from scratch. But enterprise contracts are stickier than consumer subscriptions by almost every historical measure.

I am genuinely uncertain which model compounds better over a ten-year horizon. The $950B suggests the market has an answer. I am not sure the market has seen enough data to make that call definitively.

ideas.title: ServiceNow Made AI Free. Salesforce Charges Per Click. One of Them Is Right.
ideas.trend: ServiceNow bundled AI into all product tiers at no extra cost (April 9 announcement) while Salesforce's Agentforce charges $0.10 per action; enterprise AI pricing debate active across tech and SaaS communities this week
ideas.consensus: SaaS companies are racing to add AI features to stay competitive in the agent era
ideas.angle: These are not competing feature sets. They are competing theories about what enterprise software is worth in the agent era. The bundler historically wins the enterprise renewal. History shows Microsoft ran this playbook successfully against every standalone category it absorbed.

content_pack.x_longform:
The first major move in the enterprise AI pricing war was to give AI away for free.

In April, ServiceNow restructured its entire product lineup. Foundation, Advanced, and Prime tiers all ship with AI built in. No add-on purchase. Token pools included at each tier, replenished when depleted. The logic: AI is now a feature, not a separate product.

Salesforce runs the opposite model. Agentforce charges $0.10 per action via Flex Credits. Enterprise customers deploy agents, agents complete tasks, invoices reflect exactly what ran. The logic: AI effort maps to economic output and the vendor should capture that value.

Two market leaders. Two opposite theories about what enterprise software costs in the agent era.

The choice matters because whoever sets the pricing convention captures the renewal relationship for a decade.

Per-action pricing works when outputs are easy to measure. Salesforce's model suits transactional CRM workflows: qualify a lead, resolve a ticket. Every action maps to a business event. The buyer can calculate ROI before signing and the vendor can grow revenue as volume scales.

The problem: enterprise procurement teams price unpredictability risk heavily. Per-action bills move with agent volume. Finance teams do not approve open-ended cost structures without caps. CIOs have started requiring usage ceilings before authorizing agentic deployments, per TechTarget's reporting on the ServiceNow change.

ServiceNow removed the unpredictability. Token pools are fixed at contract. IT teams forecast the AI renewal like any other software line. That trades AI revenue upside for customer trust and renewal stability.

History favors the bundler in enterprise software. Microsoft bundled Teams into Microsoft 365. Then Copilot into every tier. Each bundle eliminated a standalone category and compressed the market share of vendors who priced per unit. The per-unit vendors who survived did so by owning a workflow end-to-end.

Salesforce's bet is that Agentforce owns CRM workflows and per-action economics scale at the enterprise level. ServiceNow's bet is simpler: customers renew when the bill is predictable.

In enterprise software, the simpler contract usually wins the renewal. ServiceNow made the simpler contract.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people treat enterprise AI pricing as a product decision. I do not think it is. It is a theory about what software is worth in the agent era.

ServiceNow on April 9 bundled AI into every product tier at no extra charge. Salesforce still charges $0.10 per Agentforce action. Both companies sell into the same enterprise customer base. Both believe AI agents will transform how those customers operate. But they have made opposite bets on how that transformation should be billed.

The bundler is saying AI has become infrastructure, like compute or storage: you pay for capacity, not transactions. The per-action model is saying AI has granular economic value that maps to business outcomes, and vendors should participate in that value creation.

I find the bundler argument more convincing based on history. Microsoft bundled Teams, then Copilot, and eliminated standalone categories in the process. But I also recognize that ServiceNow and Salesforce are not the same business. ServiceNow's workflows are primarily internal IT and HR processes where individual action values are harder to isolate. Salesforce's CRM actions have cleaner dollar values attached to them.

I lean toward the bundler model winning the enterprise market long-term, but I am not certain whether per-action pricing can survive at scale. The moment a customer sees an unexpectedly large AI bill, they cap agent usage. Caps on usage become caps on the vendor's upside. I am not sure that tension is resolvable by better contract terms alone.

ideas.title: The World's Largest Staffing Firm Just Bet on Replacing Its Own Business
ideas.trend: Adecco's unlimited Salesforce Agentforce deal targeting over 50% AI-driven revenue by end 2026 is circulating in enterprise AI and SaaS repricing discussions this week as the clearest signal of incumbent capitulation
ideas.consensus: AI adoption accelerating in HR and staffing; companies adding AI tools to improve recruiter efficiency
ideas.angle: The company whose entire business model depends on placing humans in jobs committed to replacing over half its own revenue model with AI agents. When the most exposed incumbent in a sector moves fastest, the sector is repricing. Efficiency gain is not the story. Replacement is.

content_pack.x_longform:
The company most threatened by AI agents was the first to commit more than half its revenue to them.

Adecco runs the world's largest staffing operation. 27,000 recruiters across 60 countries. The entire business model earns by placing human workers into jobs.

In March, Adecco signed an unlimited Agentforce license with Salesforce through 2027, targeting more than 50 percent of revenues from AI agents by end of this year.

The largest human staffing firm in the world is betting it can automate the work that made it large. When the biggest incumbent in a sector makes that bet publicly, the clock starts for everyone else.
content_pack.x_thread:
[1/7] The company most threatened by AI agents was the first to commit more than half its revenue to them.

[2/7] Adecco runs the world's largest staffing operation. 27,000 recruiters across 60 countries. Three global business units. The entire model earns by placing human workers into jobs.

[3/7] In March, Adecco signed an unlimited Agentforce license with Salesforce through 2027, targeting more than 50% of revenues from AI agents by end of this year.

[4/7] That target is aggressive. Getting from a pilot to 50% of revenues requires replacing core staffing workflows that have operated the same way for decades.

[5/7] The UK pilot showed 15% time savings and faster placement rates. Those numbers are real. The gap between 15% time savings and 50% AI-driven revenues is where all the interesting questions live.

[6/7] Every staffing firm is watching this. If Adecco hits the target while maintaining fill rates and client satisfaction, the entire industry's cost structure changes in under two years.

[7/7] When the biggest incumbent in a sector makes that bet publicly, the clock starts for everyone else.
content_pack.substack_draft:
The staffing industry's entire value proposition is knowing where human talent is and getting it to the right place. The relationships, the market knowledge, the trust accumulated over millions of placements: these are supposed to be the moat.

Adecco, the world's largest staffing firm, just committed to running more than 50 percent of its revenues through AI agents by end of 2026. The announcement came from a partnership with Salesforce's Agentforce platform. The implied claim is that AI agents can do the matching and placement work that 27,000 recruiters currently perform.

I find the target plausible in narrow corridors. High-volume, repeatable placements and temporary work at scale look like search problems that AI handles well. The UK pilot showed 15 percent time savings in exactly that category. But 50 percent of revenues is a much larger claim than 15 percent efficiency gains, and the gap between those two numbers is where all the real questions live.

The structural question I keep returning to: if AI agents can successfully automate the core matching function in staffing, what is Adecco's business model in five years? Is it the infrastructure layer running the agents? Is it the data asset accumulated from decades of human placements? Something else entirely?

I am not sure Adecco has a complete answer. But signing the deal was a statement that sitting with the ambiguity is better than waiting to see what competitors do.
